ops.title: Hand-modeled git fakes get exit codes wrong in a consistent direction: 1 where git uses 128
ops.body:
Measured against real git 2.51 (2026-08-03) while inventorying cc-context's
`writeShipFakes` (`internal/cli/ship_test.go:33`). The fake models git's *fatal*
conditions as **exit 1**. Real git uses **128** for all of them:

| condition | fake | real git |
|---|---|---|
| `symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, no symref | 1 | **128** `fatal: ref ... is not a symbolic ref` |
| `checkout -B <b>` where a worktree holds `<b>` | 1 | **128** `fatal: '<b>' is already used by worktree at '<path>'` |
| `commit` under a held `index.lock` | 1 | **128** `fatal: Unable to create '...index.lock': File exists.` |
| `branch --show-current` in a broken repo | **128** | 128 (the one it got right) |

One right out of four is the signature of hand-modeling, and the correct
conclusion is the strong one: **treat every exit code in a hand-written fake as
unverified**, not just the ones anyone happened to probe.

Why it matters even when no arm reads the difference today: the three ship-side
callers classify with `code == 0` / `code != 0`, so 1 and 128 collapse and
nothing breaks *yet*. It is a loaded trap. `internal/vcs/trunk.go` already
reasons about exactly this split — `--quiet` turns the miss into a provable
exit 1 and leaves 128 for a git that genuinely broke — so the moment a caller
splits `case 1:` from `case 128:`, the suite validates against the lie. That is
the shape of the original incident: a fake modeled the miss as 1, a defect hid
for months behind a passing test.

Second, related failure mode from the same fake: **a fake that does not know a
verb exits with its own catch-all code**, and the caller reads that as a tool
outcome. `writeShipFakes` dispatches on `"$1 $2"` and matches only
`symbolic-ref --short`, so `symbolic-ref --quiet` and `show-ref --verify
--quiet` both fall through to `*) fake git: unmatched argv; exit 2`. Every code
path reached only through those two probes is therefore untestable through the
fake, and fails on an exit that means "the fake is ignorant", not "git said no".

Corollary for reviewing any PATH-fake suite: grep the fake's dispatch arms
against the argv production actually emits. An arm that never matches is a dead
test, and it is invisible in both the fake and the test.
